newsitem.title: GUYANA: Waves of Guyanese mourners delay Jagan's cremation.
newsitem.headline: Waves of Guyanese mourners delay Jagan's cremation.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Guyanese flocked for a fourth day on Tuesday to pay their last respects to former President Cheddi Jagan, forcing the postponement of his cremation.
Family members said Jagan's funeral pyre would be lit on Wednesday to allow mourners an extra day to see their former leader's body, which has laid in state since Saturday.

"People want to view the body and when they heard that it was going to be moved this morning there was nearly a stampede," Jagan's brother Derek Jagan, speaker of Parliament, told Reuters at the Albion Sports Ground 80 miles (130 km) east of Georgetown, where Jagan's body is lying in state.
He said the family decided to postpone the cremation when they heard that tens of thousands were still on their way to pay tribute to Guyana's most famous politician.
Guyana, with a total population of about 800,000, has virtually stood still since Jagan died of heart failure at Walter Reed hospital in Washington last Thursday.
Interim President Samuel Hinds, sworn in that day to lead Guyana until the next elections, said the official period of national mourning had been extended from six to seven days.
The tide of humanity at the Albion stadium was so great on Monday night that family members had to link arms around Jagan's casket to prevent the crowd from knocking it over.
"Be calm, be quiet, give President Jagan the respect and dignity he deserves," his widow Janet said on national radio.
Thousands continued to stream along roads in the sugar growing region towards Albion stadium late on Tuesday. Many carried small black flags or photographs of Jagan.
The outpouring of national grief appeared to have united a country deeply split by racial divides, fulfilling a dream Jagan was unable to realise in a political career spanning five decades.
Jagan, the son of indentured labourers from India, was to be cremated in a traditional East Indian ceremony at his birthplace Port Mourant, a few miles (kilometers) east of the Albion stadium.
Caribbean leaders attended a ceremony in the capital on Monday to pay their respects to a man who played a major role in Caribbean Cold War politics.
Cuba's President Fidel Castro sent a massage saying that Havana had lost a "great friend" and the Caribbean an "outstanding leader."
U.S. President Bill Clinton last week called Jagan "a champion of the poor".

A former Marxist and frequent visitor to Cuba, Jagan was Guyana's first prime minister when Britain granted its colony self-government in 1961. He led his left-leaning People's Progressive Party to a surprise election victory in 1992.
